svg.text: Proving Flame: Two Ways Gas Equipment Does It
Every gas appliance must prove a flame before it opens the main gas valve — the mechanism differs.
Standing Pilot + Thermocouple
Pilot flame heats a bimetal thermocouple
junction — generates roughly 25–30 mV.
That millivolt signal holds a magnetic
safety valve open — nothing else does.
Pilot out → millivolts die → valve snaps shut
If under ~20 mV: weak thermocouple, or pilot
flame not fully bathing the junction.
Thermopiles (250–750 mV) run whole millivolt systems, not just this circuit.
Test point: read mV at the lead under load — not open-circuit.
Electronic — Flame Rectification
Burner flame is ionized; an AC-energized
sensor rod sits directly in it.
The flame conducts asymmetrically to ground —
the control board needs a minimum microamp DC signal.
Signature failure: rod coated in oxide/grime —
flame present, current too low, locks out after ~10 sec.
Fix: clean the rod, check the porcelain insulator for cracks, and verify the
burner has a solid ground path — the circuit needs both halves to work.
Test point: read DC microamps in series with the sensor rod lead, flame lit.
Never bypass flame proving on either system — lockouts exist to prevent unburned gas
from accumulating in the appliance or the space around it.
